title: Tests, CI and the build
headline: The tests are not the bloat: 325,579 lines of tests against 768,202 of source, no snapshots, and the browser suite does not repeat the unit tests (37 of 781 end-to-end tests use no page). The waste is in how the checks run, and it is paid per push whoever uses the platform: one push type-checks the same commit five times (183 s each here, 70% of the build) and builds it four times; every unit test file first loads 1.9 MB of admin English in a fresh worker (a 187-file sample takes 90 s today and 27 s without both); lint re-reads about 6,200 files on one thread (about 3 minutes, 1 s with a cache); and 229 server modules form one import cycle that 12 import lines close. Four small changes (TC-1, TC-3, TC-5, TC-12) remove about 9 runner-minutes of repeated type checks, about a quarter of the unit run and about 3 minutes of lint per push without checking any less. Before opening is the cheap time for the two with risk: cutting the cycle (TC-2) and changing the rule for what runs before a push (TC-6, the owner's call).

clean: Nothing in this dimension argues from 'no store uses it'. Every finding is a cost per push, per build or per test run, so the owner's clarification changes no verdict here. CI cost follows commits, not shoppers; what grows at opening is the price of a late or killed deploy.
Test volume is healthy: tests are 30% of src lines; no __snapshots__ folder, no .snap file, no toMatchSnapshot or toHaveScreenshot; the largest fixture is 39 KB and the agent-eval recording 20 KB.

The end-to-end suite does not repeat the unit tests: 742 of 781 tests drive a browser page and only 37 are plain HTTP calls (my count), most of them checks that a route refuses a visitor without a session.
No single test file sets the floor of the unit run: the largest, src/db/commerce.test.ts (8,166 lines, 324 tests), runs alone in 9.7 s (timed here).
A unit run prints 9 lines when it passes (timed sample, output counted), so the test count does not flood an agent's context.

The unit tests' database is well made: 4 baseline files, a template named by a hash of the migration files, built in 5.9 s (timed here), a copy per test file in 1.1-1.5 s. Caching it in CI would save seconds.

Very little tests dead code: about a dozen source files are imported only by tests. The six *.test.ts files under docs/ are page generators with their own config (docs/site-pages/vitest.config.mts), run by hand; they are not dead tests.
A docs-only push runs nothing (ci.yml:10-14) and the content/** exception is deliberate; a run on main is never cancelled (ci.yml:27-32); the audit job needs no install.

The typing patterns the brief suspected are not what makes the type check heavy: schema.ts and its imports 573 MB, every admin catalogue 537 MB, page-content 358 MB, against about 5 GB for the whole program. The catalogues are plain object literals. The check is big because the program is big.
ESLint runs no type-aware rule and its import plugin has one single-file rule (eslint-config-next/dist/index.js:172), so lint builds no type program and a per-file cache is safe.
Browser budgets exist and run in CI: first scripts and page weight per route in e2e/performance.spec.ts:21-58.
Lazy imports in server code are an established pattern: 58 await import() calls in 30 files of src/server (rg), so cutting the cycle that way introduces nothing new.

Only one test pins CI's configuration (src/lib/ci-playwright.scan.test.ts: image tags and the list of browser jobs). No test pins the build's type check, the Vitest setup files, the lint script or the schema argument, so the fixes below fight no existing check except where TC-7 says so.
src/lib is nearly a clean layer already: 1 of its 1,146 files has a run-time import out of lib and 10 import a type from server, components, app or db.

findings.title: One push type-checks the same commit five times; three of the checks hide inside CI's builds
findings.evidence: next.config.ts:46 skips the build's type check only on Vercel, so `pnpm build` in the e2e, hosts and signed-in jobs (ci.yml:152, 206, 249) each runs it. In this machine's build the TypeScript step took 182.9 s of 262.0 s (build.log: 'Finished TypeScript in 3.0min'). Next's doc says the build checks the complete project of the tsconfig, test files included, and that typescript.ignoreBuildErrors skips the step. The static job (ci.yml:56) and the quick gate (ci.yml:302) run `pnpm typecheck` on the same tsconfig. Lint runs twice (55, 299). `pnpm db:check` runs in each of the 3 integration shards (110, matrix at 86) although it reads only the repository. With a migration pending the gate's steps are skipped, so the count is four.
findings.cost: About 9 runner-minutes of repeated type check per push in the three build jobs (3 x 183 s measured here; GitHub's runners differ), each under a 7 GB heap limit, and about 3 more where static and the gate both check. At about 35 CI runs a day that is 5 to 7 runner-hours a day (estimate). The three browser jobs each end about 3 minutes later than needed, and `release` waits for all of them, so every migration release is about 3 minutes later.
findings.who_pays: CI on every code push; the owner waits longer for a release with a migration
fix_steps: 1. next.config.ts:39-46: beside ON_VERCEL add `const SKIP_TYPECHECK = ON_VERCEL || process.env.SKIP_BUILD_TYPECHECK === "1";` and set `typescript: { ignoreBuildErrors: SKIP_TYPECHECK }`. Rewrite the comment at lines 44-45: the type check is the static job's and the quick gate's; CI's browser jobs set SKIP_BUILD_TYPECHECK; a local `pnpm build` checks as before.
2. .github/workflows/ci.yml: add `SKIP_BUILD_TYPECHECK: "1"` to the `env:` block of the jobs e2e (lines 137-141), hosts (188-195) and signed-in (233-238). Change nothing else in those jobs.
3. .github/workflows/ci.yml:109-110: give the step 'Migrations match the schema' `if: matrix.shard == 1`.

4. Words in the same change: docs/build-memory.md:30 (CI's builds no longer check; static and the gate do); the sentence in CLAUDE.md's Commands section about Vercel's build skipping the type check (add that CI's browser jobs skip it too); a commented line for SKIP_BUILD_TYPECHECK in .env.example; a decision row in docs/decisions.md; a note on step 1.8 in the Progress table of docs/audits/code-review-2026-11.md and a line in its change log.

5. Optional and separate (medium risk): lint and types once per push. In `pending`, drop `steps.status.outputs.pending == 'false' &&` from the lint and type-check steps (ci.yml:298 and 301) so they run on every push to main, with or without a migration. In `static`, give `pnpm lint` and `pnpm typecheck` (ci.yml:55-56) `if: github.event_name != 'push' || vars.AUTO_MIGRATE != 'true' || vars.DEPLOY_VIA_CI != 'true'`, so pull requests and a repository with the gate switched off still check there. `release` already requires `needs.pending.result == 'success'` (ci.yml:343), so a red lint or type check still holds a migration.
tests_and_rules: src/lib/ci-playwright.scan.test.ts reads ci.yml (Playwright image tags, the jobs that install a browser): untouched by these edits, must stay green.
src/lib/next-config-headers.test.ts imports next.config.ts and src/lib/chromium-trace.test.ts reads its text; neither looks at the typescript key (rg).

The written rule 'CI's builds still check' (docs/build-memory.md:30, next.config.ts:44-45) changes. Its purpose, a type error caught before or beside the deploy, is kept: static checks every push and pull request, the gate checks before every deploy without a migration, and `release` needs static.
CLAUDE.md, Commands: the sentence on Vercel's build. docs/audits/code-review-2026-11.md: finding FH10, step 1.8 (Open).
src/lib/env-example.scan.test.ts scans src only, so it does not force the new variable into .env.example; add it anyway, the README says the file names every variable.
findings.done_when: On the next push to main without a migration, the `pnpm build` logs of the e2e, hosts and signed-in jobs contain no 'Running TypeScript' line, the run shows `tsc` in two jobs only (static and pending), and 'Migrations match the schema' ran in one integration shard.
findings.saving: Steps 1-3: about 9 runner-minutes per push and about 3 minutes off the wall time of each browser job (from the 183 s measured here), so a release with a migration is about 3 minutes sooner. Step 5: one more type check (about 3 minutes) and one lint per push.
findings.risk: Low for steps 1 to 4. What could break: a type error that only the build's own check would see. There is none: the build checks the same tsconfig project as `pnpm typecheck`, with the same route types from `next typegen`. It would be noticed by static going red on the same push. Step 5 is medium because it touches the release conditions; test it with a push that carries a seeded lint error: `pending` must fail and nothing may deploy.
findings.already_tracked: Partly. Code review FH10, step 1.8 (Open) tracks the three cold builds. The type check inside them and the doubled lint, type check and db:check are not tracked.
findings.notes: Do steps 1 to 4 first, alone: three lines of YAML and one of TypeScript. Leave step 5 until TC-12 and TC-4 have made lint and the gate's check cheap; it then removes the last duplicate.

findings.title: 229 server modules import each other in one cycle; 12 import lines close it
findings.evidence: I rebuilt the run-time import graph of src (each of 5,909 files transformed with esbuild, so type-only and unused imports are gone) and ran Tarjan: one strongly connected component of 229 modules, all in src/server, 5.17 MB. catalog.ts, cart.ts, customers.ts, visibility.ts and checkout.ts each reach 1,305 modules (20.4 MB of source); 637 of 852 page, route and layout files reach the cycle. With the 12 import lines above cut, the largest cycle is 20 modules and the reach is catalog.ts 417, cart.ts 351, customers.ts 317, the favicon route 1,307 -> 373. A plain regex over the source (no bundler) gives the same 229 and 1,305 in 0.22 s, so the number can be held by a unit test. The verified report adds: 18 server chunks of 4,175,868 bytes identical but for their source-map name, each holding 697 modules; evaluating the cluster as one bundle takes 0.81-0.84 s and +180 MB. An import cycle already broke a route in production once (scripts/await-deploy.mjs:12-14, D440).
findings.cost: Server: a function that imports any core server module evaluates the cluster, 0.81-0.84 s and +180 MB as one plain bundle, paid per cold start; the server dimension sizes this, and it grows with traffic and with the number of functions once stores open. Tests: 18 unit and 49 integration files each load about 1,300 modules, about 55 CPU-seconds per run of both suites at the bundle's speed (estimate). The type check is not part of this cost: TypeScript follows lazy imports too. The lasting cost is that nothing stops the next import from deepening the cycle.
findings.who_pays: The server per cold start; CI and agent sessions for 67 test files; whoever next adds an import
fix_steps: 1. Put the measure in first. Add `importGraph(root)` to scripts/lib/ratchet-count.mjs: walk src, leave out *.test.ts(x), read each file's `import ... from` / `export ... from` / bare `import "x"` lines with a regex, skip `import type`, `export type` and clauses whose names are all `type`, resolve `@/` and relative paths, run Tarjan; return `largestCycle` and `catalogReach` (modules reachable from src/server/catalog.ts). Write both into src/server/ratchet.baseline.json through scripts/ratchet.mjs and assert them in src/server/ratchet.scan.test.ts the way the other numbers are: a rise fails, and a fall fails until the baseline is lowered. Today's values: 229 and 1,305.

2. Move four pure helpers to src/lib, where their callers are synchronous: `firstNameOf` (src/server/notifications.ts:455-461) to a new src/lib/first-name.ts; `lookOf` (src/server/theme-shots.ts:349) to src/lib/theme-shots.ts; `PLATFORM_INSTALLS_MAX` (src/server/platform-theme-installs.ts:41) to a new src/lib/platform-theme-installs.ts; `agentProblem` (src/server/shopping-agents.ts:42-50) to src/lib/shopping-agents.ts (it needs `featureOn` from src/lib/store-features.ts and the Store type as a type import). Each old module re-exports the name so other importers keep working. Point shopper-emails.ts:38, design-presets.ts:64 and :69 and seo.ts:7 at the lib modules.

3. Turn the async calls into lazy imports inside the function that calls them (the pattern of src/server/bonus.ts:435): pages.ts:43 -> `const { keepOwnRuleIds } = await import("./visibility")` at line 318; shopper-emails.ts:38 -> notificationOn and templatedSlots at 314-316, 498-509 and 638; taxonomy.ts:26 -> checkedRules and namedByRules at 199-202, ruleMemberIds at 418 (keep the two types as `import type`); customers.ts:17 -> eraseSubject at 500; custom-fields.ts:57 -> refreshStoreFieldSearch at 184, 198, 214 and refreshFieldSearch at 463; seo.ts:4, 48, 55 -> listIndexedEntries (604, 689), themeStoreCards (603, 650, 984), getPlatformPageRoles (602, 798); orders.ts:22 -> providerOf at 503; design-presets.ts:64, 69 -> askForThemeShots (825, 2368), themeShotsFor (151), platformInstallCount (1270, 1280).

4. One edge, or one file's edges, per commit. After each: the tests beside the two modules, then `pnpm test src/server/ratchet.scan.test.ts`. After the last: `node scripts/ratchet.mjs` to lower the baseline; expect largestCycle 20 and catalogReach 417.

5. After each deploy, scripts/await-deploy.mjs already calls every outsider route once (its SMOKE_CHECKS, D440's lesson). Also open one storefront page, one admin page and /sitemap.xml on production, since seo.ts and pages.ts are on those paths.

So the English costs 0.13 s a file and the fresh worker 0.21 s a file. findings.title: The type check is one 8,003-file program: 3 minutes and a 7 GB heap limit, with no single type to blame

Tests and e2e are 39% of the project's own syntax trees and 24% of the whole program by characters. fix_steps: 1. No decision needed for the cheap half: do TC-1, TC-3, TC-12 and TC-5 first. They cut the cost of the present rule (lint to seconds after a session's first run, the unit run by about a quarter) without changing what is checked.

C: the local rule of B with the gate unchanged; the full unit suite reports beside the deploy, as the integration and browser suites do today.
4. Write the choice where the rule is written: CLAUDE.md:12, README.md:57, docs/capacity.md:97, a decision row, and step 0.2's note in the code review's Progress table.

ci.yml:40-42 says why the gate is one job (each job is a runner to wait for): option B keeps it one job and makes it longer.
package.json:12 `test:smoke` is named in ci.yml:305 and in CLAUDE.md's Workflow paragraph ('the money tests, D526'); option B changes both.

4. The third budget is the import ratchet of TC-2 (largest cycle, reach of catalog.ts).

An experiment, on Vercel only, measured under an 8 GB cgroup cap as docs/build-memory.md did: add `serverSourceMaps: false` to the ON_VERCEL spread at next.config.ts:82, then `enablePrerenderSourceMaps: false`. Keep a switch only if the capped peak falls by 0.3 GB or more, and add the row to the table in docs/build-memory.md. findings.title: CI keeps nothing between runs except pnpm's store
findings.evidence: Each job's only cache is setup-node's `cache: pnpm`. tsconfig.json sets incremental and .gitignore:40 ignores *.tsbuildinfo, so every type check in CI starts cold. Vitest 5's fsModuleCache defaults to true and writes node_modules/.vitest-cache; CI starts empty. The verified report put the Vitest half at about 3 CPU-seconds, the time esbuild needs for every file. My cold-against-warm samples under Vitest say more: 22 component files took 24.0 s cold and 16.3 s warm (1,521 modules), 41 unit files 10.9 s and 8.4 s (394 modules), about 5 ms a module. The unit tests reach 3,461 modules, so about 17 to 22 s of a cold unit run is transform (estimate). Still small.
findings.cost: Every type check starts from nothing on each of about 35 CI runs a day: 183 s here per check. Vitest's transforms cost roughly 20 s of each cold unit run and less in each integration shard (estimate from the samples).
fix_steps: 1. After TC-1 and TC-8 (the recorded seconds). In `static` and `pending`, after `pnpm install`, add a cache step for `tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` (and `tsconfig.app.tsbuildinfo` once TC-4 exists) with key `tsbuildinfo-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml', 'tsconfig*.json') }}-${{ github.sha }}` and restore-keys `tsbuildinfo-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml', 'tsconfig*.json') }}-`.

2. Compare the recorded type-check seconds of ten runs that restored the file with ten that did not. Keep the step only if the median falls by a third or more; otherwise remove it and write the result in the decision.

findings.title: Lint reads all 6,213 files on one thread every time, with no cache: about 3 minutes, and it is on the deploy path
findings.evidence: package.json:9 is `eslint --max-warnings 0`: no --cache and no --concurrency, though the installed ESLint 9.39.5 has both (its --help; concurrency defaults to off). ESLint walks everything but .next, out, build, next-env.d.ts and .claude (eslint.config.mjs:9-17): 6,213 lintable files by find (5,910 in src, 236 in e2e, 37 in scripts). Timed here on every fifth file of src, e2e and scripts (1,235 files), one thread: 36.4 s and 40.5 s, so about 3 minutes for the whole tree (estimate from the sample; it fits the gate's written 5 min 11 s for lint, type check and smoke tests). With --concurrency auto: 26.5 s and 32.1 s. With --cache --cache-strategy content: 37.6 s to fill the cache, then 1.0 s for the same files, twice; the cache file is 515 KB. The config has no type-aware rule and the import plugin's only rule is no-anonymous-default-export (eslint-config-next/dist/index.js:172), so a file's result depends on that file and the config alone.
findings.cost: About 3 minutes of one core per lint (estimate): twice per push in CI (static at ci.yml:55 and the gate at :299, the second before the deploy hook), and once before every push in each agent session (CLAUDE.md:12). At about 35 CI runs a day that is about 3 runner-hours a day, nearly all of it on files that did not change.
findings.who_pays: CI on every push; the owner in minutes before each deploy; every agent session before each push
fix_steps: 1. package.json:9: `"lint": "eslint --max-warnings 0 --cache --cache-strategy content --cache-location node_modules/.cache/eslint/"`. That folder is ignored by git and by ESLint already; the unit tests' database template is kept beside it.

2. .github/workflows/ci.yml: in `static` and `pending`, after `pnpm install`, add a cache step for the path `node_modules/.cache/eslint` with key `eslint-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml', 'eslint.config.mjs') }}-${{ github.sha }}` and restore-keys `eslint-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml', 'eslint.config.mjs') }}-`. The content strategy compares file hashes, so a fresh checkout's new file times do not empty the cache.
3. Optional: add `--concurrency auto` for the cold run (a session's first lint, a changed config): 21 to 27% less on the sample.
4. Words: one clause in CLAUDE.md's Commands list (lint keeps a cache in node_modules/.cache/eslint; delete the folder to lint from nothing) and a decision row.
tests_and_rules: No test reads the lint script (rg for 'max-warnings' and 'pnpm lint' in src/**/*.test.ts finds nothing).
CLAUDE.md:12, README.md:57 and docs/capacity.md:97 (lint before every push) are kept; the rule becomes cheap.
ESLint drops a cached result when its config or version changes, so a Dependabot bump (.github/dependabot.yml, weekly) re-lints everything.

Code review step 4.1 will move import bans into lint with no-restricted-imports, a single-file rule: the cache stays valid. A cross-file rule (import/no-cycle) or a type-aware one would not be; such a rule must run in a second, uncached eslint call.
findings.done_when: A second `pnpm lint` on an unchanged tree finishes in under 15 s on the machine where the first took minutes, and the gate's lint step takes under 30 s on a CI run that restored the cache (read from the step's time, or TC-8's summary).
findings.saving: From about 3 minutes to seconds for every lint after the first: on the sample, 1.0 s for 1,235 unchanged files against 36 to 40 s. Per push that is about 2 to 3 minutes off the deploy gate, the same off static, and the same off each agent push after a session's first (estimate).
findings.risk: Low. A stale pass could hide an error only if a rule read other files; none does today (checked in the config). What would show it: `eslint --no-cache` disagreeing with the cached run; run that now and then in a scheduled workflow if wanted.
findings.notes: Missed by the report, which called lint 'not measured'. Confidence is high on the sample's times and medium on the whole-tree total, which is the sample times five. One line in package.json gives agents the saving at once; the CI cache step gives it to the gate.

findings.title: Each test file that opens the database spends half a second importing Drizzle and the schema, one small module at a time
findings.evidence: Vitest gives each test file a fresh worker (isolate defaults to true; the integration config also runs files one at a time, vitest.integration.config.mts:16) and loads packages from node_modules natively, module by module. A probe in scratch, 20 one-test files per variant, one niced worker, warm cache, two or three runs each: an empty test 1.9-2.1 s; a test importing @/db/client 11.3-11.9 s; the same packages without the schema 8.2-8.6 s; drizzle-orm/node-postgres alone 7.2-7.8 s, which is 0.27 s a file over empty against 57 ms in plain Node; drizzle-orm alone 4.7-4.9 s; pg 2.2-2.5 s; zod 2.6-3.0 s. With Vitest's dependency optimizer told to pre-bundle drizzle-orm (test.deps.optimizer.ssr, enabled, include drizzle-orm and drizzle-orm/node-postgres), drizzle-orm/node-postgres falls to 2.4-2.6 s and the client's packages without the schema to 3.4-3.6 s. By the import graph 525 of 556 integration files and 25 unit files load src/db/client.ts. No test mocks drizzle-orm (rg).
findings.cost: 0.48 s per file for the client today, 0.07 s with the schema gone (TC-5) and Drizzle pre-bundled. For 525 integration files that is about 250 s of a serial run, about 85 s of wall time in each of the 3 shards on every push; about 0.25 s a file of it is Drizzle's own modules (estimate from the probe; real test files and CI runners will differ).
findings.who_pays: CI's integration shards on every push; agents running pnpm test:int
fix_steps: 1. After TC-5. vitest.integration.config.mts: inside `test` add `deps: { optimizer: { ssr: { enabled: true, include: ["drizzle-orm", "drizzle-orm/node-postgres"] } } }`. Put the same block at the root of vitest.config.mts so the projects of TC-3 inherit it (25 unit files open the client).
2. Time one shard before and after on the same machine (`pnpm test:int --shard=1/3`, Vitest's duration line), then run the whole integration suite and the unit tests of src/db.

3. If a test fails because two copies of drizzle-orm meet (one pre-bundled, one loaded natively by a package Vite does not transform), add that importing package to the include list. If that does not settle it, drop the setting: do not change app code for it.

4. Turn on Vitest 5's import breakdown for one run (the `importDurations` option in its config types, `print: true`) to see whether another package costs as much as Drizzle did; pg and zod were 0.02 and 0.04 s a file in the probe.
tests_and_rules: vitest.integration.config.mts and vitest.config.mts: the only files that change. No scan test reads them.
The optimizer writes its bundle under Vite's cache folder in node_modules (ignored by git); in CI it is rebuilt each run, about a second in the probe.
CLAUDE.md's rule that integration tests run against a real database (pnpm test:int after scripts/db-setup.mjs --seed) is untouched: only how a package is loaded changes.
src/db/testing.ts (PGlite) does not import drizzle-orm, so the unit tests' database is not involved.
findings.done_when: On one machine, `pnpm test:int --shard=1/3` reports a duration at least 30 s shorter than before the change (expected: about 44 s, 0.25 s for each of the roughly 175 files in a shard), with the same test counts.
findings.saving: About 0.25 s per test file that opens the database: about 130 s of the integration run across its three shards and 6 CPU-seconds of the unit run (estimate from a 20-file probe). With TC-5 the client's import falls from 0.48 s to 0.07 s a file, about 215 s across the shards.
findings.risk: Low to medium. What could break: an identity check across two copies of drizzle-orm, or a mock of a pre-bundled package behaving differently. Either shows as a failing integration test in the trial of step 2, before anything is pushed.
findings.notes: Missed by the report, which timed the schema in plain Node only. The probe files live outside the repo and import the real client, so the per-file numbers are real, but the trial on a shard is the proof. The same half second is not paid in production: the app is bundled there.

findings.title: A push that changes only tests builds and deploys production again
findings.evidence: The push filter leaves out only *.md and docs/** (ci.yml:10-14). Every other push to main runs `pending`, which after the gate calls Vercel's deploy hook (ci.yml:317-325), and the hook builds the head of main; vercel.json has no step that skips a build. Nothing looks at what changed. In this clone's history 75 of the last 92 commits with files run CI, and 6 of those 75 (8%) change only test files (*.test.ts, e2e/**, e2e-live/**): 74179fc, 7b59c18, 07cec9b, fe454bc, 0bce04f, 9f7ea0b. The deployed app cannot differ after such a push: no route imports a test file.
findings.cost: About one deploy in twelve rebuilds an unchanged app (estimate: 8% of commits, and a commit is not always a push of its own): a Vercel build at the 8 GB edge (docs/build-memory.md:44-46) that prerenders 1,426 pages again, and a `pending` runner that waits for it, up to 20 minutes. About 3 a day at today's pace (estimate from about 35 CI runs a day).
findings.who_pays: The build on Vercel; CI's pending runner while it waits
fix_steps: 1. .github/workflows/ci.yml, job `pending`: before the gate, a step `changed` that lists the push's files (`git diff --name-only ${{ github.event.before }} ${{ github.sha }}`, after fetching the `before` commit) and writes `deploy=false` when every file matches `\.test\.tsx?$`, `^e2e/`, `^e2e-live/`, `^test/` or `^src/test/`. A forced push or a `before` that cannot be fetched writes `deploy=true`.

2. A guard in the same step: read /api/health as scripts/await-deploy.mjs does; if production does not report the push's parent commit (or a later one) as live, write `deploy=true`, so a test-only push after a failed deploy still brings production up to date.
3. Add `&& steps.changed.outputs.deploy != 'false'` to the `if` of the deploy-hook step and of the wait step (ci.yml:318 and 327). The gate's lint and type check still run: they cover the tests too.

4. Words: the comment block at ci.yml:260-272, the Workflow paragraph of CLAUDE.md ('Pushes of *.md and docs/** alone run nothing' gains: a push of tests alone is checked but not deployed), docs/ci-migrations.md, a decision row.
tests_and_rules: CLAUDE.md, Workflow: a push to main deploys (D5), and each deploy waits until /api/health reports the commit (D389). A skipped deploy must skip that wait too, or the job fails after 20 minutes.
D530 (the hook builds the head of main, so the ledger is read again before the call): the new condition sits beside that check and does not replace it.
src/lib/ci-playwright.scan.test.ts reads ci.yml's job texts for browser installs only: unaffected.
The pattern list must not include scripts/ or .github/: scripts/next-build.mjs and the workflow do change what is built and deployed.
findings.done_when: A push that changes one *.test.ts file shows `pending` green with the deploy step skipped while /api/health still reports the previous commit; a push that changes one non-test file under src deploys as before.
findings.saving: About 8% of deploys (estimate): at today's pace about 3 Vercel builds a day, each several minutes of an 8 GB build machine.
findings.risk: Low to medium. A wrong pattern would hold back a real change. Noticed by: /api/health lagging main after a non-test push; the guard of step 2 and the next code push both repair it.
findings.notes: Small and true. Not worth a change of its own: do it when ci.yml is open for TC-1. It matters a little more after opening, when each needless deploy is also a moment of cold functions for real visitors.
